item.title: When Every Day Feels Like Trauma
item.description:
When you think about trauma, it’s usually framed as an isolated event. Something that has happened to you that has caused a great deal of havoc on your emotions and on other parts of your life. But for some people, trauma isn’t isolated to a singular event or something easily pinpointed. Some people feel like they’re going through trauma every day, which can make ordinary experiences feel dangerous and overwhelming.

Understanding Chronic Trauma

Chronic trauma is something experts call complex trauma or C-PTSD, and it’s more common than you might think. It stems from prolonged, repeated, or inescapable traumatic events. It’s seen in cases of ongoing abuse or neglect, particularly in childhood. The intense feelings you get when you are going through trauma stretch beyond a singular event to affect core emotional regulation, relationships, sense of self, and even bodily functions.

Here’s the part that often surprises people, at least those who aren’t experiencing it. Not everyone who feels constantly on edge has experienced abuse, neglect, or any clearly identifiable traumatic event. Sometimes trauma-like feelings don’t come from a singular trauma at all. It comes simply from living in a world that can be unnervingly unpredictable, relentlessly demanding, and downright exhausting.

Causes of Chronic Trauma That Aren’t Related to a Single Trauma

There are several ways that you can develop chronic trauma symptoms that aren’t directly related to a singular traumatic event.

Your childhood environment contributes to how you process the world around you as an adult. If you grow up in a household that demands perfection, has high expectations, or doles out subtle criticism, your nervous system learns to stay alert.

Through experience, you have learned to always anticipate what’s next or what could go wrong as a protective shield against negative consequences. This learned nervous system response will continue into adulthood and will manifest as perfectionism or overwork.

Chronic stress in adulthood can have a similar effect on your nervous system. Long-term financial struggles, high-pressure jobs, caregiving responsibilities, or even living in a community where safety is uncertain can all contribute. These stressors train your body to stay in a state of high alert. While these stressors aren’t as definable as a catastrophic ordeal, they can make daily life feel like a test of endurance. Triggers that seem harmless to most can send you reeling.

Even experiences that feel normal on the surface, such as balancing school, work, and family, can contribute to this state. When life demands more than the energy you have, your nervous system can mistake these chronic pressures for real threats. This creates a loop of hypervigilance, shaping the way that you respond to situations emotionally, physically, and even spiritually.

Feeling Unsafe

One of the hardest parts of living with chronic stress or trauma-like symptoms is the disconnect between your reality and your internal perception. While you may not be in any actual danger, your mind and body perceive your circumstances as potentially harmful.

This disparity is often what puzzles the people in your life and can make your reactions to normal stressors seem like an overreach. On the outside, things might appear stable. You have a job, a home, and supportive people in your life. You may even have a faith that you hold dear. Yet, inside your body, hidden behind that confident smile, your body feels unsettled, guarded, and tense, as if danger is imminent.

This internal (and what seems like eternal) sense of unsafety can be confusing and even discouraging. But it’s important to realize that while your brain may be capable of logical thought, your nervous system isn’t.

Your nervous system doesn’t measure safety through a logical method but relies on experience to gauge danger. If your body has learned that pressure, responsibility, or unpredictability are constant, it may struggle to relax even when the present moment poses no threat.

Responding, Not Reacting

When your nervous system is stuck in survival mode, reactions tend to come faster than reason. You might find yourself snapping at people, emotionally shutting down, overthinking, or withdrawing before you even realize what’s happening. These reactions are protective and are your body’s attempt to keep you safe based on past patterns, not necessarily present-day reality.

To fully overcome your trauma symptoms, you must move away from reaction and into thoughtful and deliberate positive responses. One healthy response comes through self-awareness. Instead of judging yourself harshly for your reactionary tendencies, reframe your response to ask yourself what it is that your body is trying to protect itself from. What is the perceived danger?

While it might seem obvious to you when you slow down your body and mind, the perceived threat might not always be at the forefront of your mind while you’re experiencing your trauma responses. Over time, you’ll begin to see exactly what you’re fearing or feeling threatened by. And when you understand what the threat is, you can work toward neutralizing the threat and overcoming your fear.

This mental reframing will also shift you from self-criticism to curiosity. You can shift ideas like I’m so out of control or “I am always so nervous because I’m always in danger to mere curiosity.” Instead, you could reframe it to “Why am I always nervous when there’s no immediate threat?”

God of Peace

Isn’t it wonderful to know that the God of all Creation, the Prince of Peace Himself, is an active, loving Father who wants to interact with you? It’s comforting to remember that God sees every moment in your life, even the ones where you’re weary and struggling with hidden pain, even when others overlook the pressure you feel because it’s not like traditional trauma.

When you pause and reframe before you react, you open a place where God can meet you. Matthew 11:28-30 extends a beautiful invitation to us. It tells us to come to Jesus when we are burdened. To come to Him when we are weary. And He will give us rest. What an awesome gift rest is to those who have hypervigilance or chronic stress.

When you’re burdened, turn to Him. A quick prayer or a spontaneous song of worship can make a big difference in how you feel. Not only are you inviting the creator of peace into your stress, but you are unloading your burden straight onto His loving and broad shoulders.

Therapy can help

Many people who feel chronic stress but who haven’t had an obvious trauma shy away from therapy. They hesitate to seek help because they believe their stress doesn’t qualify them for professional therapy. They believe that because their trauma experience isn’t clearly defined, they aren’t actually victims of its snares.

But therapy isn’t reserved for worst-case scenarios. It’s a private, safe space where you can start to understand why your body and mind are responding to everyday life in the way they are. You can explore how to interrupt the default emotion of stress in non-threatening situations.

Understanding your chronic stress is the first step toward healing. Your hypervigilance is a signal of perceived danger. It acts as a sign that it’s time to slow down and listen to what your nervous system has been trying to tell you.

If you’re living in survival mode and have been for a long time, learning how to rest can feel uncomfortable and unfamiliar at first. Feeling safe can be relearned. As your body and mind learn how to respond to triggers and stress predictably and healthily, you will start to respond neutrally to things and situations that trigger you now.

This is your invitation and permission to pay attention to your mind and body. Take one intentional step toward stripping away the unexplained trauma in your life. Call our offices to set an appointment with a counselor. A therapist can help you understand your trauma and responses and give you tools that can help you live a fuller, more peaceful life.

item.title: New Women’s Insecurities Brought About by the Digital Era
item.description:
As long as we can remember, women have had to face insurmountable hurdles and overcome great impediments that have contributed to women’s insecurities for centuries.

Women across the world have had to fight for basic human rights such as voting, owning property, and walking without an escort. Sadly, some of our fellow women are still fighting for these rights in other parts of the world to this day.

However, the 21st century has generally brought about a significant reduction in some of these practices against women. Many traditional practices and beliefs that traditionally contributed to women’s insecurities, like gender bias, workplace inequalities, gender-based violence, and social stigmas, were issues modern women thought were behind us.

But just when women had begun to walk in light of this progress, a new and unexpected challenge has emerged, reviving women’s struggles with insecurities yet again.

The Rise of the Digital Era

The digital era, also known as the Digital Revolution or Information Age, began in the mid-twentieth century. It has been marked by the transition from traditional industries to an economy centered on information technology. This has had a profound impact on women, bringing both opportunities and challenges.

Opportunities the digital world has opened for women include:

Economic Empowerment Digital technologies have opened new job opportunities, particularly in tech and remote work, allowing women to balance work and family responsibilities more effectively.

Education and Skills Development Online learning platforms have made education more accessible, enabling women to acquire new skills and advance their careers.

Entrepreneurship The internet has provided a platform for women entrepreneurs to start and grow businesses, reaching global markets with minimal investment.

Advocacy and Activism Social media and digital tools have empowered women to advocate for their rights, raise awareness about gender issues, and mobilize support for social causes.

While the opportunities are immense, the tech era has also introduced new insecurities for women, impacting various aspects of their lives. From biased algorithms to enhanced cybersecurity threats and everything in between, this whole new era is piling on a new set of pressure for women than ever before.

Unexpected Tech-Related Concerns that are Increasing Women’s Insecurities

AI and Algorithm Biases There is already evidence that many of the AI technologies and algorithms being developed can perpetuate gender bias and negative stereotyping. When this technology is applied to hiring processes, women have unfortunately fallen short.

Some studies have shown that job hiring algorithms favor men for technical roles while steering women toward positions requiring skills that are typically lower paid. These job imbalances can make women undervalued or unfairly judged based on biased data.

The Imposter Phenomenon A feeling of not belonging is a common experience for women when it comes to the tech industry. It has been exacerbated by the industry’s gender imbalance, the fast-paced nature of the tech industry, and the high visibility of male tech achievements while female achievements are suppressed.

For example, the gross underrepresentation in tech leadership roles has left many feeling like they aren’t as adequate or competent as their peers in tech.

Rise of Cybersecurity Threats Statistically, women have been targeted more aggressively in cyberattacks such as deepfakes, doxxing, and online harassment. Women who experience online humiliation and cyberbullying can have a pervasive sense of insecurity and fear about their online presence and suffer significant emotional distress, anxiety, and even PTSD.

How Tech-Related Insecurities in Women Manifest

  • Body Image Issues
  • Increased Privacy Concerns
  • Social Isolation
  • Overcompensation
  • Self-Doubt
  • Reluctance to Speak Up

The prevalence of social media platforms has amplified unrealistic beauty standards. Women often feel pressured to conform to these ideals, leading to issues like body dysmorphia, low self-esteem, vulnerability, and fear. To counteract their insecurities, some women may overcompensate by working excessively hard, striving for perfection, or taking on more responsibilities than necessary.

Women in tech may also frequently question their skills and knowledge, feeling as if they aren’t as competent as their male counterparts. This often leads to reluctance to take on challenging projects or apply for leadership roles.

The digital age has blurred the lines between work and personal life, making it challenging for women to maintain a healthy work-life balance, resulting in increased stress and burnout.

All these new women’s insecurities in the digital world highlight the need for greater understanding, dialogue, and resources to help women navigate the digital landscape confidently and safely. There is a need for more inclusive practices and support systems in the tech industry to help women feel secure and valued.

Possible Strategies for Women to Overcome Tech-Based Insecurities

Maintaining work-life balance in the digital age can be challenging, but there are several effective strategies to help manage. Setting clear boundaries, like specific work hours, ensures that everyone in your life knows and respects your personal time.

Other ways to help navigate the complexities of the digital age while maintaining a healthy work-life balance include:

  • Prioritizing ourselves and making time for activities that promote our well-being, such as exercise, cherished hobbies, and relaxation. Regular breaks and physical activity can help mitigate the effects of digital overload.
  • Negotiating flexible work arrangements that suit us as women and mothers and can allow a balance between work and personal commitments. Demanding validation of our unique needs as women, such as flexible hours or remote work options, is not a sign of weakness but rather empowerment.
  • Learning how to use technology mindfully by leveraging productivity tools to manage our time effectively and eliminate the potential for digital distractions. A good tip is to set specific times to check messages, emails, and social pages to avoid constant interruptions.
  • Scheduling regular times for digital detox is crucial to help us as women unwind and unplug from social and work-related technology. This can help to recharge and maintain a healthy balance between being always on and having personal peace of mind.
  • Being realistic and practical about what we can achieve in a day and avoiding overcommitting does not make us less of a woman but rather promotes our wholeness. We don’t have to be “Wonder Woman,” and it’s okay to say no when necessary to prevent burnout and to accept that we don’t have to do extra to prove our worth.

Understanding and addressing these new digital-related issues that are increasing women’s insecurities requires a multifaceted approach, including promoting digital literacy, creating supportive online communities, and advocating for more inclusive practices in tech industries.

As a woman in this fast-paced digital landscape, it’s okay to admit that you need to seek support to get over any hurts and insecurities that you feel. Overcoming tech-related insecurities can be challenging, but professional help can make a significant difference.

Here are some options to consider:

  • A career coach who specializes in tech can provide guidance on career development, skill enhancement, and overcoming workplace challenges.
  • A mentor you can find in your field can provide invaluable support and advice. Mentors share their experiences, offer guidance, and can help you navigate the complexities of the tech industry.
  • An occasional professional development workshop or training session, focused on building technical skills and soft skills, can boost your confidence. Such programs often include networking opportunities, which can also help reduce feelings of isolation.
  • A support group for women in tech can provide a sense of community and shared understanding. Support groups offer emotional support, practical advice, and a platform to share experiences.
  • An online program to bolster your skills on various tech topics is a great morale booster. Enhancing your skills through these courses can help you feel more competent and confident in your abilities.
  • A mindfulness activity like meditation, yoga, or stress management techniques can help you manage anxiety and build resilience.
  • A therapist or counselor can help you explore the root causes of your insecurities, develop strategies to build confidence, and address negative thought patterns.

Women’s insecurities about tech-related matters are more common than any of us may believe, but nothing to be ashamed of.

If you have more questions or would like to talk to a professional about which of these options is best suited for you, you can find specific resources or professionals right here on this website. Call the numbers you see here today.

item.title: Habits That Make Loneliness and Depression Worse
item.description:
It’s perfectly normal to sometimes feel alone, vulnerable, and in need of connection, support, and validation. Many people go through seasons of feeling this way until their situation changes, and they find the help they need. However, others seem to live their lives in a constant state of loneliness and depression, forever frustrated that they can’t seem to connect with anybody, and clueless as to how to change.

Loneliness is not about being alone as much as it’s about feeling unseen and as if you don’t matter. This might have started in childhood, when your needs and wants were dismissed or overlooked by someone who should have been nurturing and loving you. It might be the result of recent trauma that has left you feeling as if you no longer know how to participate in society.

Regardless of the root cause, you have likely picked up habits over the years that have contributed to your feelings of loneliness and depression. You are not forever stuck in this situation, but there is work to do if you are going to get out of it.

When Loneliness and Depression Leave You Feeling Invisible

If you are dealing with loneliness and depression, you might feel as if you are a ghost. It is as if people see through you and as if you make no real impression on anyone around you. This is an awful feeling that you can never get used to, no matter how many years you have experienced it, and you should never have to. People are made for connection, friendships, relationships, and interdependence.

Life is supposed to be complicated and sometimes messy, busy, challenging, and comforting. We are meant to have our hearts broken and then mended, to have love and to give it, to provide support to others, and to receive when we are broken. If you are missing out on these things, you are not to blame.

There could be any number of reasons as to why you are struggling. However, nothing changes until you make it change. It always pays to examine your life and consider what you can do differently.

Habits That Make Loneliness and Depression Worse

People who deal with loneliness and depression are usually stuck in freeze mode. You might have tried to fix your situation, to make friends, and to build relationships, only to fail and feel worse about yourself. Now you are stuck coping with your feelings and doing everything you can to numb your emotions.

So many common, seemingly harmless habits make loneliness and depression harder to deal with. Things like doomscrolling endlessly on your devices, binge-watching shows late into the night and on weekends, and overworking are all valid ways to unwind. However, at some point, these habits are simply keeping you from making changes in your life and are not helping with your underlying issues.

You might be able to stave off feelings of hopelessness and loneliness for the night, but ultimately, you will have to make some changes if you are going to have a breakthrough. Consider the following habits that you might be engaging in, and how you can begin to make changes.

Repressing Your True Feelings

At the root of loneliness and depression for many people is the feeling that no one truly cares. There is a cycle to loneliness and depression that looks a little something like this: you feel as if no one sees you or cares about you, so you isolate and withdraw from all social interactions. Since you have withdrawn from people, they don’t see you, and it logically follows that you feel unseen.

When you are in a social situation, even in a workspace, you remain closed off and silent. The people around you either assume that you are uninterested in connection, even polite interest, or that you are quiet because you are content.

Lonely people dealing with depression don’t often appear to be lonely or depressed. They paste smiles on their faces, pretend to be confident, and convince themselves that they are fine. This is a form of emotional dishonesty, and it is the exact opposite of intimacy and connection.

It’s risky to let people into your life and to share your struggles. There are instances and occasions where it would be inappropriate to wear your heart on your sleeve, such as in a professional environment. It isn’t helpful to withdraw all the time. You will never connect with someone meaningfully until you can be vulnerable and honest about your emotions and battles.

Downplaying Your Needs

Have you ever found yourself agreeing to do something you would rather not do, only to feel resentful and bitter about it afterward? Perhaps you feel as if you can’t let others down, despite constantly being let down and disappointed yourself. People who deal with loneliness and depression will often downplay their preferences, needs, and wants.

When you have a decade or more of unmet needs, you will naturally feel as if you are not worth anyone’s time or effort, or as if your needs and preferences matter less than others. In the end, you will feel less worthy of love and attention, and isolated with a host of genuine needs that have gone unmet.

It takes time and practice to find your voice and speak up for yourself, but you can start by asking yourself what you need, what you want, and what you prefer. This can apply to any situation.

For example, you might like to have a quiet morning at work with minimal small talk. You have every right to inform your colleagues that you are focusing on your tasks, but that you would love to hear their stories later during your lunch break. Each time you value your needs, preferences, and wants, you are giving something deeply important to yourself, kind of like watering a dry and thirsty plant.

Bristling

Although you don’t want to face most of your feelings, there is one feeling that will constantly surface, and that is anger. Anger is not always a bad emotion to feel; in fact, most people feel angry when they experience something unfair or unjust. When you are overlooked, unseen, and unheard by those around you, it is understandable and even logical to be angry.

While you may not express your emotions, others often feel your anger in interactions with you. You may appear irritable, short-tempered, sharp, or cold. It is not your intention to communicate these things, but many people will keep their distance from you because of your bristling demeanor.

Most people who deal with loneliness and depression have been policing their tone and adjusting their body language for a long time. It is exhausting and ineffective as far as making connections goes.

The only way to become emotionally honest with yourself and others is to face your emotional needs. The problem is not the anger you feel or the prickly way you communicate with those around you. That is a symptom of deeper emotional needs that have gone unmet for too long.

A Better Solution for Loneliness and Depression

The reason these habits don’t help in the long run is that they are not about changing your situation; they are about coping with your feelings. In the end, your feelings are numbed and suppressed, and you are stuck in the same situation that caused your loneliness and depression in the first place.

Loneliness and depression are soul-crushing things to deal with. However, you are not a victim, and you don’t have to remain in your current situation. Regardless of how things feel now, there is a brighter future ahead of you if you will only begin to help yourself.

One of the best things you can do if you are dealing with loneliness and depression is to get counseling. It would be my honor and deepest goal to provide a safe space for you to express yourself and journey with you for as long as you need support. Please consult with my reception team if you would like to investigate further.

I’m cheering you on!
